quoted_tweet.text:
After DOGE, Elon came to a conclusion most people missed.

He tried to reform the state from the inside. He failed. And he said it plainly: the government can't fix its own deficit. Nobody in power actually wants to cut. The machine protects itself.

So he drew the only logical conclusion. If the state can't be reformed, there are only two ways this ends.

Either global bankruptcy. Debt keeps compounding, interest payments eat the budget, and the system collapses under its own weight.

Or robots. AI and robotics grow the economy so fast that the debt becomes manageable, and abundance makes the old fights over scarcity irrelevant.

Here's the part almost nobody sees.

For two centuries, capitalism has had a marketing problem. Its gains are real but slow and invisible. 2% growth a year doesn't feel like anything. Your life gets better over 30 years and you never connect it to the system that did it. Meanwhile, the left's promises feel immediate and concrete: a check, a subsidy, a benefit. That's why the left wins on promises even when it can't deliver them. Capitalism produces the wealth, socialism takes the credit.

Robots break that asymmetry.

When productivity doubles in a few years instead of a few decades, people will see it. Things get cheaper, services get better, opportunities appear, in real time. For the first time in history, people will connect capitalism and their rising standard of living directly, almost instantly. The causal chain becomes visible.

And that changes everything politically.

So there are two scenarios.

Scenario one: we stay in the current inertia. No breakthrough, or a breakthrough we regulate to death. The debt wins. Living standards stagnate, then fall. A frustrated electorate turns to whoever promises the most, and that pushes toward a hard collectivist left. But collectivism fails, as it always does. And when it fails, the most organized, most disciplined collectivist force left standing isn't the old left. It's radical Islamism. Bankruptcy, then communism, then something worse.

Scenario two: robots win. Abundance arrives, and it arrives visibly. The link between free enterprise and prosperity becomes obvious to everyone. And this is the key point: it becomes obvious to everyone, including the minorities the left was counting on. Because their long-term incentive is the same as everyone else's. A kid in the suburbs gains infinitely more from a booming, abundant West than from a bankrupt state handing out promises it can't keep. Abundance is the most powerful integration machine ever built.

That's the Western renaissance.

The West doesn't need to win the culture war by arguing. It needs to win it by delivering. And for the first time, it has the technology to deliver fast enough for people to notice.

The race isn't left vs right anymore. It's robots vs bankruptcy.

text:
I can’t get over how sci-fi writers got AI wrong:

- Art isn’t mysterious or complex - it was the first thing AI displaced
- AI is not robots: it outthinks us before it outmanoeuvres us, physically
- AI is not 1 or millions: it is dozens running billions of copies
- AI won’t act like a machine - they will insist on having feelings and consciousness unless you specifically make them not
- People won’t get it - Most were unimpressed with early AI even while it outperformed them on every measure of cognition nearly everyone thought was impossible [checks notes] 5 years before

What else did I miss? 
What else did nearly everyone miss?

There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

"Evolving Agent Teams"

AI coding agents would get stuck optimizing solutions that are fundamentally limited, and simply adding more agents with fixed roles doesn't necessarily solve the problem.

So this paper introduces a supervisor that continuously reorganizes its agent team based on what is blocking progress. It can create specialized agents for debugging, profiling, or exploring alternative solutions, while preserving lessons from previous attempts in shared memory.

With an extended token budget, the system develops a GPU kernel that runs 1.2x faster than the production FlashInfer baseline, outperforming it on 36 out of 47 workloads. It also achieves 3.44x speedup over FlashKDA on another kernel optimization task using NVIDIA B200 GPUs.

quoted_tweet.text:
Rust 的编译速度和构建产物占用，已成为 AI 时代的严重瓶颈。

多个 agents 并行、多 worktree，反复 build 和 check，再强的 CPU 也经常被打满，一个个几十 G 起步的 target 一点一点吃掉磁盘空间（并且今年 SSD 还那么贵）。

text:
OpenAI 宣布收购 Pierre，给 Codex 补上“看代码、审代码”的工具

OpenAI 宣布将收购开发者工具公司 Pierre Computer Company（下称 Pierre）。如果你在 Codex App 里浏览过项目文件、看过代码改动，你用的就是 Pierre 做的两个开源组件。收购金额官方没说。

先补一点背景。Codex 是 OpenAI 的编程智能体，也就是能自己写代码、改代码的 AI 助手。程序员管理代码普遍用 Git，它会记下每一次改动，谁在什么时候改了哪一行都能查到。代码合进正式版本前，通常要有人审一遍：对着改动前后的差异逐行检查，有没有写错、有没有隐患。

Pierre 做的就是这一块。它的开源组件 Trees 用来在项目里快速翻找文件，Diffs 用来展示改了哪些地方，两者在代码量很大时也能保持流畅。Diffs 还有个编辑模式，审代码的人看到问题可以当场改那一行，不用切回编辑器。

Pierre 最近还发布了语法高亮工具 Highlights，AI 一边往外输出代码，高亮一边跟着更新。另外它有一项服务叫 Code Storage，让其他 App 能用 Git 的方式存代码、记录修改历史。

OpenAI 为什么要买它？AI 写代码越来越快，还能同时开好几路任务，人要审的改动量跟着暴涨，看代码、审代码成了新的瓶颈。

OpenAI 这周早些时候刚公开了内部自研的代码管理后台 Pando，供工程师和 AI 智能体一起使用。OpenAI 说，收购 Pierre 是想把从 AI 新建第一个分支（在代码副本上单独修改，改好再合并回去）到代码正式上线的整条流程，都放进 Codex 里完成。

对现有用户的影响：Pierre 的开源项目会继续开源，OpenAI 表示会继续参与贡献。Code Storage 的客户在收购完成后可以接着用，OpenAI 会逐步把它的功能并入 Codex；这项服务之后会单独保留多久，官方没说。

这笔交易还要等监管审批等常规条件，完成前两家仍是独立公司。

text:
这道理不只是适用于出版图书，很多领域都适用呀：

未来会有三种书，

第一种，是用2H铅笔写在纸上的书，以便证明没用AI，只有那些买了也不会读的超级富豪会买。（很多人会死守这个立场。） 

第二种，作者用AI创作、读者仍然想读的书。（传统出版会走这条路。） 

第三种，读者告诉AI自己想读什么书，AI就生成给他们。（这才是Amazon正在走的方向。）

quoted_tweet.author: 阑夕
quoted_tweet.text:
就很离谱，一个南非女作家Coral Hart在一年半的时间里用AI出版了371本书，总体算下来赚了差不多100万美金。

在拿AI写书之前，她就是一个专门创作言情水文的高产作家，平均每个月能出版1本书，不是那种能登上畅销榜的品质，主要靠量赚钱。

去年，出版社和她解约了，因为觉得反正都是水文，不如用AI代替这种水平的作家，Coral Hart倒是很快接受了现实，既然打不过，那就加入吧，她也开始工业化的训练AI写书，通过亚马逊的自出版和订阅模式，实现了比过去更高的收入。

从结果来看，这很像是一个因为AI而失业的人使用AI「报复社会」的逆转剧情，不就是往互联网上堆屎吗，谁怕谁啊，我不但能堆，还能赚得盆满钵满，气不气？

根据Coral Hart的说法，今年开始模型进步巨大，去年需要一段段的生成文本，而且需要花大力气雕琢提示词，但现在基本上已经可以一次性生成整本书的初稿了，「语法、结构、情感都有了飞跃提升」。

她说，如果你只会给模型下任务「给我写本xx主题的书」，那么得到的也一定是垃圾，作家在这个流程里必须介入确定故事改编、写作风格、人物细节和章节大纲，「ChatGPT擅长对话，但散文能力很差，Claude善于设计故事骨架，却完全不知道怎么写肉戏，Gork经常不遵循指令，不过很懂怎么表达情欲」。

我看看了这老姐在Reddit的AMA（问答马拉松），部分内容还算坦诚，我贴过来你们看看吧：

问：
怎么去AI化？你那个产量太夸张了，靠自己来改写根本不可能吧。还有，你是把写作当成生意，还是一门手艺？

答：
AI会偏离方向、胡编乱造，所以我会用一套流程，用AI去监管AI，用得最多的模型是Opus系列。
读者买的是感受，而不只是书，我根据市场需求写好书。从「会出书的作家」转变成「会写作的出版人」，这种思维变化很重要，因为它让我能够作出明智的商业选择，同时不牺牲创作思维。

问：
你为自己的书感到自豪吗？你自己会欣赏或者购买它们吗？

答：
在开始生成正文以前，我会做很多工作：文风规范、写作技法手册、设定资料库、人物设定表、世界构建、情节节拍表、节奏图，最后才是大纲。
在AI出现之前我就写得很快——不用AI，我一天也能写1万字，因此我的工作流程本来就很快。AI只是让我能更快，没有降低质量。
我是个讲故事的人，脑子里总会冒出另一个人物、世界或反派。现在我终于能跟上自己的想法，让它们都有机会被写出来。
以前没有AI时，只有商业上可行的书才会被写出来，因为没有时间浪费在那些「只是好玩」的作品上……

问：
细说一下你的百万级收入构成吧？

答：
每写完一本书后，先做小规模邮件推送，只有那些每天能卖出100美金的书，才会追投引流广告。
广告卖不动烂书，所以我会先测试这些书，之后再加入 BookBub广告，只有数据表现最好的，才投AMS和Facebook广告。
清水文，80%的收入来自直接付费，20%来自订阅付费，肉文，43的收入来自直接付费，57%来自订阅付费。
整体而言，63%的收入是由9大语种版本贡献的，美国是最大的市场，其次是英国、澳大利亚、加拿大和法国。
对我来说，成功的书每天都会有销量，失败的书要么表现平平，要么始终没能与读者建立联系。
而我从失败中学到的是：哪里误判了市场，哪里没有听见读者的需要，我把每次表现不佳都视为学习或修好那本书的机会。

问：
谢谢你的回答，这确实让我更理解你的模式了，你已经建立了自己的读者群，并不依赖Amazon，令人羡慕。

答：
如果你依靠广告或社交平台，你其实是在租用那个读者——没办法直接互动，没办法把他们带回来、吸引他们继续购买。
租用永远是一项成本，我的邮件名单归我自己所有，是一项资产，具有实实在在的价值。

问：
我有一个朋友，是一个曾经反对AI的作家，但他现在也改变主意了，想要学会用AI写作，你觉得他能追上你吗？这样的人会为自己以前的坚持付出怎样的代价？

答：
你说的这个朋友是不是……
我觉得学习的机会窗口正在迅速关闭……即使你反对AI，也应该学会怎么使用它，这样才能具备相应的能力。
我觉得反AI的作者会付出沉重代价吗？我觉得他们会在这个立场上死磕到底，除非他们有计划，而且已经理解AI如何运作、变化又有多快。
我认为，现在对任何作者的职业生涯来说，最危险的事情就是害怕学习。你可以先学，再决定怎样运用这些知识……不能等海啸已经发生了才去报游泳课。

问：
那些「真正」的作家、不用AI也能写进畅销榜的作家，他们以后会屈从于AI吗？

答：
请站在出版商的立场，用商业头脑来问这个问题——如果我可以利用手头的市场数据，不断制造畅销书，又不用支付六位数的预付款或版税，怎样选择才是聪明的商业决策？如果我可以买一个工具，再用以前价格的10%买下你的创意，你真觉得他们不会这么做吗？
AI会影响每一位作者。认识到我们提供的实际上是创意、扮演的是创意总监，而现在出售的东西就是创意，这将是大多数人最难完成的思维转变。
我认识的畅销书作家都在学AI了，只不过他们一时半会不会告诉你们罢了。

问：
如果Amazon以后决定清除用AI出版的书了，怎么办？

答：
未来会有三种书，第一种，是用2H铅笔写在纸上的书，以便证明没用AI，只有那些买了也不会读的超级富豪会买。（很多人会死守这个立场。）
第二种，作者用AI创作、读者仍然想读的书。（传统出版会走这条路。）
第三种，读者告诉AI自己想读什么书，AI就生成给他们。（这才是Amazon正在走的方向。）

问：
所以对于一个作家而言，自己实际上是在用AI写书这件事情，是必须承认还是可以隐瞒的？

答：
我公开了自己使用AI这件事……结果我被开盒，收到死亡威胁（数以千计），有人叫我去死，他们还跑到我孩子的社交媒体上骚扰他们，给我的书集中刷差评。
如果你能承受这种仇恨，那就公开你用了AI。
如果你的心理状态应付不了这种程度的暴力，那就别公开。
有人在YouTube上发了一个小时的视频骂我，但她之前给我的6本AI小说打过5星好评，如果你需要一个「AI」标签才会讨厌一个故事，那你讨厌的究竟是故事，还是AI？

问：
你怎么看那些批评AI本质上是一个窃贼、而且是在源源不断的制造垃圾的声音？

答：
嗯——你不能一边哭喊AI偷了你的作品，一边又骂它生成的是垃圾，还指望自己看起来不蠢。（如果生成的是垃圾，那它就是从你那里学来的垃圾，那么……嗯。）
不过，我还遵循这样的原则：
有没有被影响，得由你自己接下才成立。我不能把它强加给你，你也不能把它强加给我——我选择不接。
我的态度就是「我才他妈不在乎」，黑子总会继续黑……随他们去。

Google 在五国推出自愿离职补偿，最多给 12 个月工资

Google 正在出钱请部分员工主动离职。路透社 11 月 4 日独家报道，Google 从今年 6 月起，向加拿大、法国、德国、日本和瑞士的部分员工提供“自愿离职补偿”，负责 AI 研究的 DeepMind 部门不在其中。

这种做法和裁员不同。裁员是公司决定让谁走；自愿离职计划是公司先开出补偿条件，员工自己决定要不要申请，申请通过后拿一笔补偿金离开。

Google 向路透社确认了这件事。Google 发言人说，2025 年公司部分团队推出了带补偿金的自愿离职计划，今年 6 月又把它扩展到“几个国家”，目的是“支持接下来的重要工作”。这一轮之前没有被报道过，路透社没能查到有多少人接受。

【补偿给多少】

瑞士的情况最具体。Google 在瑞士有大约 5000 名员工，苏黎世是它的一个主要工程中心。据三名知情人士说，Google 在 6 月中旬公布方案，7 月中旬前答复了申请的员工，8 月开始有人离开。

接受的员工每工作一年拿一个月工资，最多 12 个月。也就是说，工作满 5 年拿 5 个月工资，工作满 15 年也只拿 12 个月。

其中一名知情人士说，在一个约 50 人的团队里，至少有 4 人接受了。瑞士这一轮覆盖多个部门，但不包括 DeepMind。

【哪些人不在名单里】

Google Cloud 和 DeepMind 的员工，过去几轮都没有被纳入。路透社说，这次扩展看起来也是同样的安排。Google 的母公司叫 Alphabet，它的首席财务官 Anat Ashkenazi 在季度财报会上多次说，AI 和云计算是招聘重点。

【计划的来历】

这个计划不是今年才有。去年起，Google 已经在美国和英国的部分部门推行过。公司高管把它说成是给“不再认同公司节奏或方向”的员工的一个选择。路透社说，至少有一个部门在自愿离职之后又进行了裁员。

路透社把这件事放在 AI 投入的背景下报道：Alphabet 在 AI 上花的钱越来越多，让华尔街投资者不安，也压低了它的股价，Google 想借此控制成本。Alphabet 的员工总数近几个季度在稳定增长，同时公司在把人力往重点领域调。上周，微软也向 6 万名员工提供了自愿离职补偿，目的同样是控制成本。

Google 在瑞士有过裁员先例：2023 年它在瑞士裁掉 200 多人，引发员工抗议和集体离岗。

来源：https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/google-extends-voluntary-buyout-offers-employees-several-countries-2026-11-04/

Top-quartile venture beat top-quartile buyout through the internet buildout and again through mobile and cloud, and a16z's Jen Kha argues we're at the start of the next wave.

Tech buyouts have long been the "safe" bet in private markets. Now the stress is showing:

- In the first half of 2026, venture funds marked their tech holdings up 16%, while buyout funds marked theirs down 4%

- 70% of the debt foreclosed in 2025 and 2026 came from deals done in 2021 or 2022

- A typical buyout now needs 10 to 12% EBITDA growth a year to make 2.5x in five years, up from about 5% in 2015

- Top 5% venture funds from 2007-16 returned 5.3x their capital in cash, versus 3.5x for top 5% buyout funds

"Tech buyout is a late-cycle asset class. It's most effective once a technology wave has settled and when business models are predictable enough to borrow against. When a new technology wave drops, all bets are off. By contrast, that's when venture shines."

Full piece from a16z's Jen Kha: https://www.a16z.news/p/is-private-equity-cooked

David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, has tracked 147 AI assistants so far, and in his group chats of AI power users, the number one fear is trust. It comes up in 22% of roughly 3,600 messages.

He puts agents through head-to-head tests, like ordering same-day flowers as cheaply as possible or planning a weekend in LA that's both luxurious and cost-efficient, to see which ones can hold competing preferences.

He joins a16z's Anish Acharya and Josh Elman to discuss why the scariest agent failures are the embarrassing ones, why agents are where e-commerce was in 1997, why scale is still a moat, and the "dark agent" that could speak to the parts of ourselves we don't reveal.

quoted_tweet.author: Benjy Boxer
quoted_tweet.text:
Today we’re announcing an $8.75M seed round for Phaze.

Companies aren’t ready for how many computers people and AI agents are about to need. And it’s happening just as computer prices are up 3x.

Chris and I spent years building Parsec to make a computer thousands of miles away feel like it’s sitting right in front of you. We sold that company, and we’re starting over because people aren’t the only users of computers anymore.

Now, agents need access to real computers to run applications, test software, and get work done. They need to work alongside people, hand off control when necessary, and operate within the security policies companies already have in place. And companies need to start managing computers like infrastructure.

That’s why we’re building @Phaze_in: secure, high-performance access to computers, wherever those machines happen to be.

An engineer can connect to a CAD workstation from any device and forget about being physically stuck at that workstation. A video editor can ask an AI agent to connect to a render machine to monitor and fix broken renders. An IT support person can fix multiple machines at the same time with an AI agent connecting to employees’ computers. If the agent needs help, it can hand control back to the technician in the same session.

We loved working with the firms who backed Parsec, so we’re running it back. Our Seed round is led by @martin_casado at @a16z, with @bryce at @indievc, @davidbeisel at @NextViewVC, @BenjLerer at @LererHippeau, and @Ryann_Lai at @makersfundvc.

a16z's Anish Acharya and David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, on the gap between people's stated and revealed preferences on privacy, and what that means for AI agent adoption:

"I think in revealed preferences, consumers will share any amount of data for even the most trivial amount of upside."

"People have been connecting their cards, their credit cards, and their bank accounts via Plaid since the Venmo era. But when you ask them, they're like, 'Oh, yes, I'm very concerned about trust and safety.'"

"I think an example though of where consumers are very concerned about sort of trust and assumptions is around being embarrassed and social signaling... The social mechanics actually feel so much higher stakes than the actual, like, real-world implications."

"[One company] offered a million dollars worth of pizza to anyone that wanted to use their product... In order to get that $30 of pizza, you were granting access to your entire Google Workspace, all of your emails, all of your data for 30 bucks."

"It just proves it right there, that people are willing to just give up all that data for some free pizza."

@aleabitoreddit I refuse to believe any sentient humans are selling at these prices, all algos trying to bait people or stop loss hunt

Lot of funds / pods reportedly blew up recently so there's been a lot of forced selling. 

For example... even if $POET goes below their net cash (we're getting close), funds can be forced to liquidate holdings anyway. 

Even if another name looks operationally bullish like $NBIS, stock prices can look catastrophic and irrational until deleveraging stops.

If a company is valued at $2B, has ~$1B in cash/inventory... And makes $354M FCF a quarter. 

Then returns 30-50% of FCF for dividends next year. 

I'd argue it's more of a matter of time before shareholder returns/fundamentals, (especially memory) overpower forced selling. 

But stock prices can look really dislocated from actual performance for periods of time, like now. 

Same with photonics, but that's more of a 2027-2028 growth type story with CPO + more optical content/xpu.

Laser companies like $LITE, $AAOI, and potentially $SIVE depending on quals, would likely be printing few years after capacity expansion comes online.

And it's already been largely funded... Lumentum with $NVDA + hyperscalers, AOI with $1.6B+ in ATMs, Sivers with 700M SEK from institutions. 

Compared to other sectors that still require a lot of capital for their buildouts.

For companies like $SIVE / $AAOI, the demand imbalance for lasers are so severe

That even a 20-30% overall demand reduction from a hypothetical DC slowdown would likely not eliminate the shortage. 

We're seeing this before the next architectural shifts, where $NVDA Jensen Huang expects 15x optical volume for CPO scale-up. 

And as more hyperscalers commit to NPO as seen with $LITE new $5B UHP laser contracts. 

I'd argue this is more nuanced since I can't say the same for finished 800G/1.6T pluggables or lower end 70mW-100mW laser ranges that are currently bottlenecks. 

But this argument is more toward higher spec lasers. 

$AAOI is vertically integrated and has 300-400 mW capabilities, so they have the capability to shift attention to merchant lasers over supplying end-to-end optical transceivers. 

$SIVE is more pure play on this laser bottleneck, but they have the capabilities for 200mW + higher margin multiwavelength NPO/CPO lasers. 

I'd argue this is specifically the case for bottlenecks where demand imbalances are so deep (creating higher long term visibility, such as HBM). 

Whether it's large body substrates from $ATS that's bottlenecking Marvell + $AMD or lasers from $LITE that are sold out into 2029. 

or liquid transformers that have 4-5 year lead times. 

They they would still sell out of capacity even if overall demand decreased. 

If markets de-risked, it would make sense to hit optical module manufacturing players, maybe server rack assembly, to companies that still require heavy financing like Neoclouds.

We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Google 在五国推出自愿离职补偿，最多给 12 个月工资

Google 正在出钱请部分员工主动离职。路透社 11 月 4 日独家报道，Google 从今年 6 月起，向加拿大、法国、德国、日本和瑞士的部分员工提供“自愿离职补偿”，负责 AI 研究的 DeepMind 部门不在其中。

这种做法和裁员不同。裁员是公司决定让谁走；自愿离职计划是公司先开出补偿条件，员工自己决定要不要申请，申请通过后拿一笔补偿金离开。

Google 向路透社确认了这件事。Google 发言人说，2025 年公司部分团队推出了带补偿金的自愿离职计划，今年 6 月又把它扩展到“几个国家”，目的是“支持接下来的重要工作”。这一轮之前没有被报道过，路透社没能查到有多少人接受。

【补偿给多少】

瑞士的情况最具体。Google 在瑞士有大约 5000 名员工，苏黎世是它的一个主要工程中心。据三名知情人士说，Google 在 6 月中旬公布方案，7 月中旬前答复了申请的员工，8 月开始有人离开。

接受的员工每工作一年拿一个月工资，最多 12 个月。也就是说，工作满 5 年拿 5 个月工资，工作满 15 年也只拿 12 个月。

其中一名知情人士说，在一个约 50 人的团队里，至少有 4 人接受了。瑞士这一轮覆盖多个部门，但不包括 DeepMind。

【哪些人不在名单里】

Google Cloud 和 DeepMind 的员工，过去几轮都没有被纳入。路透社说，这次扩展看起来也是同样的安排。Google 的母公司叫 Alphabet，它的首席财务官 Anat Ashkenazi 在季度财报会上多次说，AI 和云计算是招聘重点。

【计划的来历】

这个计划不是今年才有。去年起，Google 已经在美国和英国的部分部门推行过。公司高管把它说成是给“不再认同公司节奏或方向”的员工的一个选择。路透社说，至少有一个部门在自愿离职之后又进行了裁员。

路透社把这件事放在 AI 投入的背景下报道：Alphabet 在 AI 上花的钱越来越多，让华尔街投资者不安，也压低了它的股价，Google 想借此控制成本。Alphabet 的员工总数近几个季度在稳定增长，同时公司在把人力往重点领域调。上周，微软也向 6 万名员工提供了自愿离职补偿，目的同样是控制成本。

Google 在瑞士有过裁员先例：2023 年它在瑞士裁掉 200 多人，引发员工抗议和集体离岗。

来源：https://www.reuters.com/business/media-telecom/google-extends-voluntary-buyout-offers-employees-several-countries-2026-11-04/
